definition: Acting as if you are better than other people, often with a cool, scornful manner.
example: The new manager's supercilious emails made the whole staff feel like careless children.
nuance: Supercilious stresses open, cool contempt for others, while arrogant can mean simple overconfidence without any sneer.
prompt: A museum guide answers questions from a group of visiting students.
options: The supercilious guide sighed at every question as if the students were beneath his notice.
The supercilious guide crouched down and answered each child's question with patient warmth.
The supercilious guide covered the exhibits so briefly that the students learned only surface facts.
The supercilious guide was easy to spot because of her thick, dark eyebrows.
reasons: Treating listeners as unworthy of attention shows exactly the scornful superiority the word describes.
Patience and warmth are the reverse of looking down on people.
This confuses the word with superficial; shallowness is not the same as disdain.
The word comes from Latin for eyebrow, but it describes a raised-brow attitude, not how brows look.

practice.prompt: A well-known food critic visits a small family-run diner.
options: The supercilious critic sniffed at the paper napkins and asked if anything here was edible.
The supercilious critic praised the cook warmly and asked to learn the family recipe.
The supercilious critic was so eager to please that she agreed with every opinion at the table.
The supercilious critic felt too shy and unsure of her taste to say anything about the food.
reasons: Sneering at a modest place as if it were beneath her is a clear display of haughty contempt.
Warm admiration for the cook is the opposite of looking down on others.
Eagerness to please describes an obsequious person, not someone who feels superior.
Shyness and self-doubt clash with the confident sense of superiority the word requires.
